entry.title: Fluent Bit Under the Hood: The C Engine That Ships Logs From Your GPU Fleet

link.title: Fluent Bit Under the Hood: The C Engine That Ships Logs From Your GPU Fleet

entry.content:
Training and serving large models is now a telemetry problem as much as a compute problem. Every GPU node writes journald and container logs, every inference server emits latency and throughput metrics, every fine-tuning run streams progress lines that someone downstream wants to query, replay, or feed back into evaluation dashboards. Fluent Bit was built for exactly this traffic: a lightweight and high-performance telemetry agent designed to collect, process, and forward logs, metrics, and traces from any source to any destination. It is part of the graduated Fluentd ecosystem and a CNCF graduated project, and its README reports over ten million deployments per day and more than fifteen billion downloads — reach it earned by running comfortably on tiny edge boxes and huge clusters alike.

For AI and ML infrastructure teams the agent is attractive for three concrete reasons. First, footprint: it is written in C with async I/O and coroutine-based concurrency, so it can sit on every node of a GPU cluster without competing with training jobs for meaningful resources. Second, structure: parsing raw serving logs into JSON, folding multiline stack traces, dropping noise before egress — all of that happens at the edge instead of inside your log store, which keeps downstream costs and cardinality under control. Third, routing: a single agent can fan the same records out to several destinations, shipping debug logs to Loki while metrics go to Prometheus and traces flow onward through an OpenTelemetry Collector. It coexists naturally with other shippers like Vector, each doing the part of the ingestion path it is best at.

This post is a source tour of the fluent/fluent-bit repository at master, which per the README tracks development of v5.2.0 while the stable v5.1 series lives on its own branch. We walk the data path from a file being read on disk to bytes leaving on a pooled TLS connection, in the same order as the two architecture diagrams below. Every code link points at a symbol that was verified in the actual tree, so you can open each one and read along.

Figure 1 — Fluent Bit engine overview: configuration loads plugin instances, the engine event loop drives collectors, buffered chunks flow through parsing and filtering, and the tag router hands each chunk to per-output tasks for delivery.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Boot. The CLI entrypoint main, L1606 parses flags and config files, then flb_config_init, L281 builds the service context that holds the event loop, scheduler, storage, and every plugin instance.
  • Inputs. Each source becomes an instance via flb_input_new, L326; flb_input_collectors_start, L2939 launches the fd, timer, and coroutine collectors, with descriptor events dispatched through flb_input_collector_fd, L3295.
  • A concrete collector. The tail input’s in_tail_collect_event, L367 wakes when a watched file grows and reads the new lines.
  • Buffering. Records are appended into tagged chunks by flb_input_chunk_write, L773 on top of the storage layer flb_storage_create, L663 provides, which can be memory-only or filesystem-backed for durability.
  • Parsing. Parsers are registered by flb_parser_create, L1051 with JSON and regex backends, while multiline folding in flb_ml_append_text, L707 reassembles stack traces into single logical records.
  • Filtering. flb_filter_do, L121 runs each chunk through the configured chain — for example keep/drop rules in cb_grep_filter, L286 or record rewriting in cb_lua_filter, L434, both able to address nested fields through record accessors from flb_ra_create, L271.
  • Routing. The tag matcher flb_router_match, L140 compares each chunk’s tag against output match rules, and flb_router_connect, L147 wires inputs to outputs at startup.
  • Delivery. Periodic flushing via flb_engine_flush, L198 and flb_engine_dispatch, L360 creates one task per destination through flb_task_create, L551; failures come back through flb_task_retry_reschedule, L291 armed on the scheduler’s flb_sched_timer_create, L869.
  • Observability. The agent instruments itself: flb_me_create, L215 serves internal counters over HTTP in Prometheus format, so you can monitor the monitor.

Figure 2 — Fluent Bit internals: the ingestion path from collectors to buffered chunks, the parse and filter chain, tag routing into per-output tasks with retry timers, pooled connections, and the embedded metrics exporter.

From Install to Your First Model

The quickest way to see the engine move is the README’s build-from-source quick start. The requirements are modest: CMake 3.0 or newer, Flex and Bison, and YAML plus OpenSSL headers. Then:

cd build
cmake ..
make
bin/fluent-bit -i cpu -o stdout -f 1

That single command exercises the whole left-to-right flow you saw above: the cpu input registers a timer collector, the engine loop wakes it once per second (-f 1 sets the flush interval), and the stdout output prints each record as JSON to your terminal. No config file, no daemons — one binary collecting host CPU metrics end to end.

For real workloads you will use the packaged releases instead: the documentation offers Linux packages for Debian, Ubuntu, and RHEL, Docker images, and Windows binaries. A minimal configuration that follows a training job’s log file looks like this:

[INPUT]
    Name   tail
    Path   /var/log/my-train-job/*.log
    Tag    train.job
    Parser json

[OUTPUT]
    Name   stdout
    Match  *

With that file saved as train.conf, run bin/fluent-bit -c train.conf. Every JSON line the trainer writes becomes a structured record tagged train.job, ready to be filtered, enriched, and routed. Two config concepts carry most of the weight here: the Tag assigned by the input, which is the routing key everything downstream keys on, and the Match pattern on outputs, which selects which tags each destination receives — the same wildcard matcher the router applies internally. From here the natural next step is pointing the output at your real destination — a forwarder, an HTTP endpoint, or one of the seventy-plus built-in outputs the README advertises — and letting the same agent handle GPU node logs, LLM serving logs, and system metrics in one place.

The Ingestion Path in Detail

The detail diagram separates what the overview compresses. On ingestion, the engine is not one big loop but a thin event loop coordinating coroutines: flb_coro_init sets up lightweight stacks so that collectors can block on sockets or files without consuming an OS thread each. Collected bytes land in chunks keyed by tag, and the storage layer decides whether those chunks live in memory or are persisted to disk — the difference between losing buffered lines on a crash and replaying them after restart. Inputs that prefer batching can push through dedicated worker threads and ring buffers, such as the one allocated by flb_ring_buffer_create, L42, which decouples hot-path collection from the main event loop. The multiline engine sits beside the per-record parsers because both consume raw text, but they solve opposite problems: splitting one stream into records versus merging several lines into one record. Master also layers a newer processor subsystem on top of the classic filter chain — initialized in flb_processor_init, L1236 and invoked through flb_processor_run, L1800 — which is what powers the SQL stream processing the README advertises as a key feature.

Routing, Tasks, and Reliable Delivery

Once a chunk is flushed, routing turns fan-out into bookkeeping. flb_engine_dispatch walks the routes for the input that produced the chunk and creates one task per matched output; the task owns the event chunk, tracks state, and records which outputs still owe an acknowledgement. Delivery happens on output worker thread pools, and the network layer keeps pools of reusable connections per upstream — connections are handed back for reuse by flb_upstream_conn_release, L964 rather than torn down — with HTTP/1 and HTTP/2 clients implemented side by side under flb_http_do, L2130 and TLS handled inside the connection lifecycle. When an output fails, the task is not dropped: the retry layer reschedules it with backoff on the shared scheduler, and the engine can adaptively retune flush behavior as memory pressure changes. Master even ships a dead-letter escape hatch: when filesystem storage is enabled with the keep-rejected option, the engine’s DLQ path quarantines undeliverable chunks on disk with their tag and the failing output’s name, so nothing silently evaporates during a bad deploy. This is the part of the design that matters most for AI workloads, where a training cluster can briefly saturate a log store and the shipper must ride out the outage instead of losing telemetry.

Honest Limits

A few things worth knowing before you bet a fleet on it, all checked against the README and the tree. First, the README’s performance language is qualitative — “high performance with low memory footprint” is a design goal, not a published benchmark — so treat any specific numbers you find elsewhere as somebody else’s workload, not yours; measure on your own hardware. Second, master is a development branch tracking v5.2.0; for production you should follow the stable 5.1 series rather than reproducing line numbers from this tour. Third, building from source needs Flex and Bison on top of CMake, and platform quirks on Windows and embedded targets mean the packaged releases are the lower-friction path. Fourth, writing a new plugin in C is a real engineering task — the supported extension surfaces are Lua for filters and Go for outputs, which covers many but not all customization needs. Finally, it is a shipper, not a store: there is no local querying story beyond durable buffering and redelivery, so plan a destination that can answer questions, such as Loki for logs or Prometheus for metrics.

Where It Fits in an AI Stack

In practice Fluent Bit becomes the default first hop of your telemetry topology: cheap enough to install everywhere, smart enough to structure and route data at the edge, and reliable enough to retry through broker and store outages. If you want heavier transformation at the edge, compare it with Vector; if your destination is an OTel-native world, putting it in front of an OpenTelemetry Collector is a common and well-supported pairing; and for the stores it feeds, Loki and Prometheus are the canonical log and metric backends. The source tour above should give you enough of the internal map to reason about tuning flush intervals, storage modes, and retry budgets — which is exactly where a well-run fleet separates collected data from collected noise.

entry.title: Logstash Under the Hood: The JRuby + JVM Engine That Turns Raw Logs into Searchable Events

link.title: Logstash Under the Hood: The JRuby + JVM Engine That Turns Raw Logs into Searchable Events

entry.content:
Logstash is Elastic’s server-side data processing engine. It collects events from a multitude of sources at once, parses and transforms them with a small DSL that reads like configuration, and then ships each event to a stash of your choice. For more than a decade it has been the default ingestion front door of the Elastic Stack, and even with modern challengers like Vector and the OpenTelemetry Collector it still moves an enormous share of the world’s operational data. If you have ever searched a production incident in Kibana, chances are an event chain very much like the one in this post produced those documents.

Why should an AI or ML practitioner care? Because the same machinery that feeds search also feeds models. Training corpora are born from messy operational logs; LLM serving telemetry (token latencies, refusal rates, error traces) has to be cleaned and routed before it is useful; and analytics on top of structured events is still the fastest way to answer product questions about model behavior. Logstash sits at exactly that boundary: it turns chaotic machine output into typed, enriched, routable events, optionally buffered through a durable broker such as Kafka before anything downstream commits.

This post is a source-level tour of the elastic/logstash repository at its current default branch, main. We rendered two architecture diagrams straight from the tree: one showing the end-to-end event flow from inputs through the queue to filter workers and outputs, and one drilling into the internals - agent convergence, config compilation, the Java execution engine, queues, the dead letter queue, and the monitoring API. Every symbol and line number below was verified with grep against the actual tree before publication, which matters because this codebase drifts fast.

Logstash at a glance: the Ruby agent compiles configs and supervises chains, while the Java hot path moves batches from inputs through the queue to filter workers and outputs, with a dead letter queue for failures and a metrics API for operators.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • LogStash::Runner, L55 is a Clamp command-line class. Its execute, L266 method validates flags, loads the settings registry, and boots the agent process.
  • LogStash::Agent, L48 is the supervisor. It owns the desired state of every running event chain and converges toward it whenever configs change on disk.
  • Config text is parsed by LogStashCompilerLSCLGrammar, L4, a Treetop grammar, and compile_imperative, L23 turns that parse into executable intermediate representation.
  • Input plugins extend LogStash::Inputs::Base, L24; their register hook starts ingestion and pushes events into the queue.
  • The queue is pluggable: QueueFactoryExt, L54 picks between a memory type declared at L70 and a persisted type at L65.
  • Workers are pure Java: WorkerLoop.run, L76 spins on a do-while loop, calling readBatch(), running the compute iteration, then closeBatch() until shutdown is requested.
  • Filters extend LogStash::Filters::Base, L22; each worker invokes filter(event), L151 per event, or multi_filter(events), L170 when a plugin takes the whole batch.
  • Outputs extend LogStash::Outputs::Base, L22 and receive complete batches through multi_receive(events), L101, which is where batching to Elasticsearch, files, or brokers happens.
  • Failures are not lost: the DeadLetterQueueWriter, L106 records events that could not be processed via writeEntry, L441, tagged with the plugin name, id, and reason.

The internals view: bootstrap and settings feed agent convergence; the LSCL grammar compiles configs; Java worker loops pull batches from memory or persisted queues; plugins, the dead letter queue, and the metrics API hang off the same spine.

From Install to Your First Model

The fastest “model” you can fit with Logstash is a running event chain, and the README keeps that path short. If you are running it from source, the prerequisites are explicit: JDK 21 with JAVA_HOME set, plus JRuby 10.0.5.0 (the pinned version in .ruby-version). Then two Gradle tasks bootstrap the Ruby side:

./gradlew installDevelopmentGems
./gradlew installDefaultGems

The first installs development dependencies; the second installs the default plugins and other runtime gems. There is a documented bundler alternative (bundle config set --local path vendor/bundle, bundle install, then rake bootstrap and rake plugin:install-default) if you prefer Gemfile-based workflows.

Once bootstrapped, the canonical smoke test from the README is a one-liner:

bin/logstash -e 'input { stdin { } } output { stdout {} }'

That starts a chain with stdin as input and stdout as output. Type hello world and you get back a timestamped event, exactly as the README shows - your first end-to-end flow in under a minute. From there you would normally install real plugins with bin/logstash-plugin install ..., or, if you are packaging your own build, produce artifacts with ./gradlew assembleTarDistribution or ./gradlew assembleZipDistribution. For production use most people just grab the official binaries from the Elastic downloads page, but the source path above is genuinely usable, and it is the only way to debug the engine internals we are about to discuss.

The Queue: Memory or Persisted

Every event chain passes through a queue, and Logstash gives you two very different implementations behind one setting. The memory queue is a JRuby extension wrapping a Java ArrayBlockingQueue - JrubyWrappedSynchronousQueueExt, L43 extends the common wrapped-queue base and holds a blocking queue field directly. It is fast, allocation-light, and completely volatile: restart the process and unacknowledged events are gone.

The persisted queue is a different animal. Queue.java, L104 implements a page-based disk log: events are appended to pages, reads return batches with a limit and timeout, L639, and durability is tracked by Checkpoint, L28, which records page numbers, sequence numbers, and element counts so recovery knows exactly what was acknowledged. Workers drain it through the acked read client - JrubyAckedReadClientExt, L41 extends QueueReadClientBase and materializes QueueBatch objects for the worker loop.

The trade-off is the classic write-ahead-log one: the persisted queue buys you crash-safe ingestion with at-least-once semantics at the cost of disk I/O and checkpoint overhead on every ack. It protects you from Logstash restarts, not from the host disappearing - that is what an external durable buffer is for, which is why so many serious deployments put a broker in front of the engine and treat the local queue as a shock absorber rather than the system of record.

When Events Fail: The Dead Letter Queue

What happens when an event cannot be processed - a mapping conflict, a malformed date, an output that rejects the record? Logstash’s answer is the dead letter queue. DeadLetterQueueWriter, L106 is a final class implementing Closeable that appends rejected events into timestamped segment files on disk. Each record is written through writeEntry(event, pluginName, pluginId, reason), L441, so every quarantined event carries provenance: which plugin failed it and why.

Writers are not created ad hoc by plugins; they are handed out by DeadLetterQueueFactory.getWriter, L83, a static registry keyed by id that also enforces size limits and flush intervals. The engine even has a dedicated periodic poller (the DeadLetterQueue poller in instrument/periodic_poller/dlq.rb) that samples DLQ storage so the monitoring API can report on it.

Operationally, treat the DLQ as a first-class queue, not a trash can: it fills with exactly the events your transformation logic misunderstood, which makes it the highest-signal dataset you have for debugging config changes. Replay tooling exists, and the segment format is plain record files, so a small script can re-inject corrected events - but the discipline of reviewing it after every schema change is what actually keeps data loss near zero.

Observability for the Observer

A data engine that cannot explain itself is a black box, and Logstash takes its own medicine here. The Collector, L28 aggregates counters and timers into a namespaced snapshot backed by a tree-shaped MetricStore, L26. Worker loops increment consumed and filtered counters directly as they process batches, and periodic pollers extend the picture: a JVM poller samples heap and garbage collection, the PQ poller samples persisted-queue disk usage, and the DLQ poller covers quarantine volume.

All of it is exposed over HTTP. The agent constructs LogStash::WebServer.from_settings, L89 at startup and runs it on a background thread; the Rack app is assembled in webserver.rb at L147, and the NodeStats module, L21 serves the /_node/stats JSON snapshot that most dashboards consume. The API is plain JSON rather than a native scrape format, so shipping those numbers into a TSDB usually means a small bridge - the OpenTelemetry Collector with a filelog/http receiver, Vector with its HTTP source, or a cron job pushing into InfluxDB or VictoriaMetrics all work without touching Logstash itself.

The nice property is symmetry: the same snapshot that your monitoring consumes is what the engine prints when a chain wedges, so the numbers you alert on are the numbers you debug with.

Honest Limits

This tour was verified against the main branch tree, and several things deserve plain talk:

  • The engine is not the product. This repository holds Logstash core; the hundreds of real plugins (grok, http, the Elasticsearch output) live in separate repositories under the logstash-plugins GitHub organization, each published as its own Ruby gem. Clone this repo and you get the engine, its default plugin set via Gradle, and not much else - plugin bugs mean cloning a different repo.
  • The dev stack is heavy and the README says so. You need JDK 21 plus a specific JRuby (10.0.5.0), a Gradle bootstrap before the first bin/rspec run, and the README itself recommends the Drip launcher specifically because “the slow JVM startup problem” hurts during development. It also warns Drip does not work with STDIN-based configs.
  • No performance claims were verified. The README carries no throughput or latency benchmarks, and neither does this post. Sizing a Logstash deployment is an empirical exercise; anyone quoting numbers at you is extrapolating.
  • Single-node durability. The persisted queue protects one process on one host. High availability comes from the deployment pattern (redundant shippers, broker in front, load-balanced outputs), not from the engine itself.
  • The DSL is a language. The LSCL grammar is powerful but has quoting and escaping edge cases, and its errors surface as parse failures at startup rather than as friendly diagnostics at edit time.

None of these are disqualifying - they are the price of a decade-old JVM engine that prioritizes compatibility. Know them, and the architecture above will make sense every time you open logstash.yml.

entry.title: Grafana Mimir Under the Hood: HA Dedup, Tenant TSDBs and Sharded Block Reads in Go

link.title: Grafana Mimir Under the Hood: HA Dedup, Tenant TSDBs and Sharded Block Reads in Go

entry.content:
Every serious ML platform eventually hits the same wall: metrics. A modern inference fleet — hundreds of replicas across a dozen models, each exporting request latency, GPU utilization, KV-cache pressure, token throughput and queue depth — outgrows a single Prometheus long before it outgrows its GPUs. Prometheus is deliberately a single-node system, and once its head block saturates, you are stuck choosing which services deserve monitoring and which do not. Grafana Mimir is the open source answer to that ceiling: a Go codebase that the README describes as “a scalable long-term storage for Prometheus”, speaking the same remote-write protocol and the same PromQL, but spreading both ingestion and queries across a shared-nothing cluster. Metrics are only one leg of the observability triad — traces and logs complete the picture — but they are the leg every autoscaler and SLO dashboard leans on, which is why the metrics database is usually the first component to demand a distributed rewrite.

The pitch matters for AI infrastructure because fleet load is spiky and lumpy. A model launch can double active series overnight; a batch-evaluation night can triple query load. Mimir’s design absorbs this by scaling each role independently — add ingesters for more write throughput, store-gateways for more read fan-out, compactors for deeper history — all backed by object storage instead of exotic local hardware. The README reports internal testing “up to 1 billion active time series”, and equally important for operators, the whole system can start as a single binary: “Using its monolithic mode, you can get Grafana Mimir up and running with just one binary and no additional dependencies.”

This post is a source tour, not a feature list. We read the actual Go code on the main branch of four load-bearing components — the distributor (write front-end with high-availability dedup), the ingester (per-tenant TSDB), the store-gateway (sharded reads from object storage), and the compactor (block merging and garbage collection). Both diagrams below were generated from the repository tree itself, so every file box maps to a path that exists in the repo.

Figure 1 — the remote-write journey: from the single mimir binary through HA dedup and tenant TSDBs into object storage, then back out through ring-sharded reads and compaction.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Everything starts in one binary: main, L82 wires whichever components the comma-separated -target flag selects; monolithic mode runs all of them in one process.
  • The write front-end is Distributor.Push, L2284, a stateless layer that validates each remote-write request per tenant and forwards it onward.
  • Before forwarding, prePushHaDedupeMiddleware, L28 collapses duplicate samples from HA-replicated Prometheus servers so exactly one copy is stored.
  • The ingester accepts writes in PushWithCleanup, L217 and appends samples into a per-tenant TSDB head (userTSDB.Appender, L205) protected by a write-ahead log.
  • Once the head is cut into two-hour blocks, shipper.Sync, L108 uploads finished block directories to the object store.
  • On the read side, StoreGateway.syncStores, L396 keeps each store-gateway responsible for a ring-assigned subset of tenants, and BucketStore.Series, L577 streams series and chunks straight from the bucket.
  • The compactor merges block generations in runCompactionJob, L257, while BlocksCleaner.cleanUser, L452 deletes blocks nothing references anymore.

Figure 2 — the detail view: HA dedup internals, the ingester lifecycle from appender to shipper, store-gateway block syncing with lazy index reads, and the compactor's metadata-driven flow.

The Distributor: One Copy of Every Sample

Run two Prometheus replicas for availability and you immediately have a new problem: both push the same series, so a naive receiver stores every sample twice and averages become lies. Mimir’s distributor solves this with high-availability dedup keyed on two configurable labels. findHALabels, L725 extracts the HA cluster and replica labels from each series; whichever replica is currently elected leader for a cluster is tracked in a shared KV store by checkReplica, L563, and the per-sample verdict comes from checkSample, L746 — accept if this replica leads, reject otherwise. The logic lives behind two interchangeable strategies: the per-sample path in perSampleDedupe.dedupe, L84 and a newer per-request variant in pkg/distributor/ha_dedupe_per_request.go. The middleware wrapper in ha_dedupe.go chooses between them, so the choice is a config decision, not a code fork. After dedup, Distributor.Push, L2284 uses the consistent-hash ring configured by toRingConfig, L64 to ship each request to the ingesters that own the series, with replication happening by ring placement rather than by application logic. One implementation detail worth noticing: the election state does not live in any single distributor. ReplicaDesc implements memberlist.Mergeable (ha_tracker.go, L65), so the leader map can be gossiped between distributors with memberlist or held in a central KV store, and every replica converges on the same answer without adding a coordination round-trip to the push path.

The Ingester: A TSDB Per Tenant

The ingester is where samples become durable-ish: each tenant gets an isolated userTSDB with its own head block, WAL and on-disk blocks, constructed by newIngester, L416. Isolation is the whole point — one runaway tenant cannot push another tenant’s WAL past its budget. Back-pressure is explicit: checkInstanceLimits, L190 rejects pushes once in-flight requests, bytes or per-instance series cross their configured limits. The hot path, pushSamplesToAppender, L516, feeds samples and histograms into the TSDB appender with per-tenant validation, and the write-ahead log makes a crash survivable before anything is uploaded. Compaction is a background service: compactBlocks, L345 cuts the head into two-hour blocks and runs local compaction levels, while shipBlocks, L56 periodically pushes finished blocks toward object storage through the zone-aware shipper. After a block ships, the ingester can drop it from local disk — local storage becomes a cache of recent history, not the archive. Memory discipline extends to teardown as well: an idle tenant’s TSDB is detected by isIdle, L520 and eventually closed, so a platform with thousands of small tenants does not pin thousands of head blocks in memory forever.

Store-Gateway: Sharded Reads from Object Storage

Queries older than the ingesters’ lookback need the bucket, and the store-gateway is the sharded service that serves them. NewStoreGateway, L146 wires a ring, a bucket client and a registry of per-tenant stores; ring ownership decides which gateway handles which tenant, and syncStores, L396 creates or removes those stores as ring membership shifts. Each tenant store is a NewBucketStore, L203, whose syncBlocks, L309 keeps the in-memory block list aligned with the bucket index. The clever part is laziness: blocks are not copied locally in full. When a query arrives, StoreGateway.Series, L408 fans out to BucketStore.Series, L577, which consults ExpandedPostings, L82 — postings are expanded against a cached index header, then only the required chunk ranges are fetched over HTTP range requests. For an inference fleet whose dashboards hammer a few dozen series out of millions, this selectivity is what keeps reads cheap at billion-series scale. The index reader also caches aggressively: expanded postings fetched by fetchCachedExpandedPostings, L171 survive between queries, so repeated dashboard panels mostly hit memory rather than the bucket.

The Compactor: Merging Blocks into History

Left alone, object storage would fill with two-hour crumbs. The compactor turns crumbs into history. NewMultitenantCompactor, L380 builds a ring-sharded service where each compactor owns a set of tenants. Its work starts from metadata, not data: SyncMetas, L111 fetches and deduplicates block metadata, GarbageCollect, L136 marks superseded duplicates for deletion, and jobs are planned per compaction grouping. The heavy lifting is runCompactionJob, L257, which downloads a group of blocks, merges them into one, and re-uploads the result — gated by newBlockHealthValidationGate, L586 so unhealthy blocks are not propagated. Housekeeping lives in BlocksCleaner.cleanUser, L452, which removes blocks marked for deletion and cleans up departed tenants. The bucket index the compactor maintains is also what lets store-gateways stay in sync cheaply, closing the loop between write and read paths.

From Install to Your First Model

Getting a working metrics stack is genuinely short. First, download the release and run monolithic mode: mimir -target=all. The entrypoint main, L82 parses that target list, whose valid values you can enumerate with the -modules flag (help.txt.tmpl, L76); the flag itself is documented as a comma-separated list at help.txt.tmpl, L938. The HTTP listen port comes from -server.http-listen-port (help.txt.tmpl, L884). Second, point Prometheus — or an OpenTelemetry Collector — at the push endpoint: the constant PrometheusPushEndpoint = "/api/v1/push" is defined at api.go, L298 and registered on the distributor handler at api.go, L309. Third, verify data is flowing by querying the Prometheus-compatible API, which is served under the /prometheus URL prefix configured at api.go, L95 — your GPU-utilization panels now survive ingester restarts. For production, split -target values across a cluster and point block storage at S3 or GCS; wiring the deployment with a Kubernetes operator is covered in our /prometheus-operator/ tour, while the tracing counterpart for the same fleet is /tempo/, its log sibling is /loki/, and the alternative bucket-architecture comparison is /thanos/.

Honest Limits

This tour reads four pkg subdirectories plus pkg/api from the main branch; the querier, query-frontend, ruler and alertmanager services are unexamined, and the query path beyond the store-gateway is out of scope. We traced the per-sample HA dedup strategy in depth; the per-request variant exists in the tree but was not followed line by line. The HA-tracker discussion also assumes some KV-store backend holds the leader map — which backend (gossip-based memberlist versus Consul) fits you is a deployment decision this post deliberately leaves open. The “1 billion active time series” figure is Grafana’s own internal-testing claim quoted from the README — we ran no benchmarks of our own and none are implied. The diagrams omit the query-frontend, ruler and alertmanager for legibility. Line numbers refer to the tree as of today; the codebase moves quickly, and recent work on Kafka-backed ingest storage is visible in flags and tests. None of the claims here should be treated as sizing advice without your own load tests.

entry.title: Pyroscope: A Source Tour of Grafana’s Continuous Profiling Backend

link.title: Pyroscope: A Source Tour of Grafana’s Continuous Profiling Backend

entry.content:
Anyone who has served a large language model in production knows the feeling: the GPU sits at 97% utilization on your dashboard, yet tokens per second quietly sag during the evening peak. Dashboards built on metrics from Prometheus tell you that something slowed down; they rarely tell you which function is responsible. Continuous profiling closes that gap. Instead of a handful of counters, it records always-on samples of where CPU time and allocations actually go — stack frame by stack frame — for every process in the fleet, at a fraction of the cost of running a debugger.

That capability matters enormously for AI and ML infrastructure. A Python inference server wrapped around a C++ runtime spends time in surprising places: tokenizers, vendored HTTP layers, CUDA driver calls, serialization glue between the scheduler and the model. A training loop that leaks a copy-per-step shows up as a memory flame graph that grows without bound. Even the Go binaries that typically sit in front of your models — gateways, routers, token-bucket rate limiters — have hot paths worth watching. With a profiler like Pyroscope running always-on, these hot spots surface as flame graphs you can diff over time, not as anecdotes you reproduce under a debugger after the incident.

Grafana Pyroscope is the open-source continuous profiling backend in the Grafana observability stack, alongside logging with Loki and tracing with Tempo. Its 2.0 release made a bold architectural call: profiles are written directly to object storage, removing in-memory ingesters and local disks from the default path — simplifying operations and lowering resource usage at scale. We cloned the repository, read the Go source, and traced one profile sample from the HTTP push endpoint all the way to a flame graph. The two diagrams below were generated from the actual code layout.

Pyroscope at a glance: ingestion fans out through a distributor, the v2 write path lands segments in object storage with a raft-backed metastore index, and queries are planned across blocks and merged into flame graphs.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Push endpoint. Every profile arrives at the push API. RegisterDistributor, L276 wires the endpoints, and a capture wrapper can sample incoming profiles for debugging (registerPusher, L17).
  • Distributor.Push, L326 is the workhorse. It parses each raw pprof sample with a hard cap on decompressed size (RawFromBytesWithLimit, L103), rejects batches that exceed per-tenant body limits, and enforces ingestion rate limits before anything is stored.
  • Router.Send, L89 then picks a write path per tenant: the new segment-writer path, the legacy ingester path, or both during migration.
  • Segment writer. On the v2 path, profiles land in ordered write shards (segmentsWriter, L44) that feed in-memory heads (Head.Ingest, L80). Periodically each segment flushes (segment.flush, L221): heads are concatenated into one block file, the block is uploaded, and its metadata is registered.
  • Metastore. Block metadata is committed through a raft-replicated index. IndexService.AddBlock, L71 fronts the handler that applies these commands to replicated state (IndexCommandHandler.AddBlock, L61).
  • Compaction. In the background, NewMultitenantCompactor, L285 plans work per tenant and leases jobs to a dedicated Worker, L84 that merges low-level blocks into bigger, cheaper-to-read ones.
  • Query frontend. On reads, the read-path router (Query, L69) splits ranges by time and hands newer data to the v2 frontend (NewQueryFrontend, L141), which fetches block metadata, builds a balanced plan, and invokes backends.
  • QueryBackend.Invoke, L101 executes the plan’s MERGE and READ nodes; the block reader (NewBlockReader, L73) fetches only the datasets a query needs and merges samples into a response.
  • Legacy path. The v1 querier still fans out to in-memory ingesters and block-serving gateways (Querier.selectSeries, L1124, NewStoreGateway, L87) — the mode many production clusters run today.

The detailed view: ingestion internals, both write paths, storage and compaction machinery, and the two query paths side by side.

From Push to Object Storage: The v2 Write Path

The v2 write path is a study in doing less, on purpose. The distributor deliberately stays thin: parse, validate, route. Parsing is where the first hard engineering constraint appears. Profiles arrive gzipped inside protobuf envelopes, and decompression is a memory-amplification risk when tenants push large batches, so RawFromBytesWithLimit, L103 refuses payloads once the decompressed size crosses a per-tenant limit — the distributor counts discarded bytes and profiles into distinct metrics so you can see the policy biting.

Routing is the second constraint. The write-path router exists because the codebase must serve two storage architectures simultaneously. A tenant on the v2 path gets its series sent to segment writers; a tenant still on v1 gets the classic dskit ring treatment; and the combined path duplicates writes so tenants can migrate without a cutover. This is the same philosophy that lets Mimir and Loki evolve their storage without breaking clients: the write API stays frozen, the machinery behind it changes.

Inside the segment writer, the design revolves around sharding by tenant and service name. Each shard is a single-writer loop — ordered, contention-free — that accumulates samples in an in-memory head keyed by dataset. When the head grows large enough or old enough, the flush sequence in segment.flush, L221 concatenates dataset heads into a single block file, appends the tenant dataset index built by NewDatasetIndexWriter, L53, encodes block metadata, uploads the result through the object-storage bucket abstraction (Bucket, L14), and finally registers the block with the metastore. Only after that commit is the data durable and queryable — everything before is replayable in-memory state.

The bucket abstraction is what makes deployment boring in the good sense. A factory (NewBucket, L21) constructs clients for S3, GCS, Azure, Swift, or a filesystem, so a lab setup and a global fleet differ by configuration, not code. If you already run a MinIO endpoint for model artifacts, the same object store can serve your profile blocks — one more reason this architecture pairs well with an existing /minio/ deployment.

The Metastore and Compaction: Small Files Are the Enemy

Object storage is cheap per byte and expensive per request. A busy cluster writing one small segment per writer-shard per interval would generate a request storm, so compaction is not optional hygiene — it is the mechanism that keeps query-time request counts sane. The metastore records each block with a compaction level; the multitenant compactor plans which groups of blocks can merge, and a separate worker executes the merges, rewrites block files at the next level, and reports the new metadata back through the metastore’s compaction service (NewCompactionService, L29).

Separating planning (a ring-sharded, stateful component) from execution (a stateless worker that leases jobs) is a deliberate scaling choice: compaction throughput can be scaled independently of cluster ownership. The metastore itself is raft-replicated, which is notable — many metadata layers in this ecosystem lean on external stores like etcd or object-storage-backed catalogs, while Pyroscope keeps its block index as a self-contained, strongly consistent service.

From Install to Your First Model

The fastest path from nothing to a live flame graph is a single container: docker run -it -p 4040:4040 grafana/pyroscope. On macOS or Linux, brew install pyroscope-io/brew/pyroscope followed by brew services start pyroscope does the same via Homebrew. If you prefer binaries, download the archive from the latest release, tar xvf pyroscope_*.tar.gz, and run ./pyroscope. The server listens on port 4040.

Now feed it profiles. For a Python model server, add the Python SDK and point it at your process — the repository carries runnable examples under examples/language-sdk-instrumentation/python, alongside Go, Java, Ruby, Node.js, .NET, and Rust examples. For fleet-wide coverage without touching code, Grafana Alloy can pull profiles, and OTLP ingestion accepts profiles from OpenTelemetry-compatible sources such as the OpenTelemetry eBPF profiler — handy when your GPU hosts are otherwise instrumented through the /opentelemetry-collector/. Query side, open Grafana Profiles Drilldown: with the OSS stack it is pre-installed, and you can start from a service selector, pick a profile type (CPU, allocs), and scrub the timeline. If you already run Grafana with /loki/ for logs or a tracing backend for spans, profiles complete the picture: logs tell you the error, traces tell you the slow span, and the profile tells you the line of code that burned the CPU inside that span.

A useful habit for AI workloads: record a flame graph of your inference server at a known-good token throughput, then diff it against a slow period. The delta is usually a handful of frames — a fallback tokenizer path, a retry storm in a client library, a Python-level preprocessing loop — and it appears in minutes, not after a reproduction hunt.

The Legacy v1 Path Still Matters

Why does the old architecture still occupy so much of the tree? Because migrations are long and the operators are real. In v1, Ingester.Push, L336 routes to per-tenant instances (newInstance, L32), each wrapping a local PhlareDB database (New, L117) that ingests into an in-memory head (NewHead, L83), flushes parquet-backed blocks, and ships them to shared storage (Shipper, L76). Queries then fan out to ingesters for recent data and to store-gateways for historical blocks, with bidirectional streaming merge clients pooled per ring (NewIngesterPool, L36). Reading both paths is genuinely instructive: the v2 segment writer is essentially the distillation of everything the team learned running PhlareDB at scale.

Honest Limits

Continuous profiling is sampling, so very short, rare execution spikes can slip between samples; the picture is statistical and strongest for steady-state behavior. The 2.0 architecture is new — the README notes existing v1 deployments opt in via a flag and migrate without data loss, which means mixed-fleet operation and its router complexity are your reality for a while. The v2 write path assumes object storage; there is no local-disk default anymore, so even a modest single-node deployment needs a bucket endpoint (the filesystem provider covers the simplest cases). The README’s quick start is a single local container; running the microservice modules in production means operating rings, the metastore’s raft cluster, and compaction workers — real operational surface, documented in the upstream deployment guides rather than bundled into one command. And licensing is AGPLv3, which some organizations need to review before embedding Pyroscope in a commercial offering. None of these are reasons to skip profiling; they are the costs of a backend that treats profiles as first-class, queryable data at fleet scale.
entry.summary: A source-level tour of Grafana Pyroscope's v2 architecture: distributors, segment writers, object storage, the metastore, compaction, and the query path that turns pprof samples into flame graphs for AI and ML infrastructure.

entry.title: Inside Apache SkyWalking: A Source Tour of the OAP Server That Watches AI Infrastructure

link.title: Inside Apache SkyWalking: A Source Tour of the OAP Server That Watches AI Infrastructure

entry.content:
Modern AI infrastructure is a distributed-systems problem wearing a lab coat. One “ask the model” request can cross a gateway, a queue, a vector database, and a GPU inference service — and when latency spikes, someone must find which hop burned the milliseconds. Apache SkyWalking, the Apache Software Foundation’s observability platform, exists for exactly that diagnosis: it collects traces, metrics, logs, and events, aggregates them in a backend called the OAP server, and serves results through a UI and a GraphQL API. Most Java-based AI serving stacks — Spring Boot gateways, gRPC front ends, Kafka consumers feeding batch inference — are pure JVM workloads, so a Java-native APM is often the fastest way to see what your AI platform really does at runtime. And because the same platform also ingests OpenTelemetry data, the Python and Go services around the JVM can join the same topology instead of living in a separate monitoring silo.

This post is a source tour of that backend. We read the master branch of apache/skywalking and follow one story through the Java source: telemetry arrives at receivers, is dispatched into Open Assessment Language (OAL) analysis, merges through two levels of in-memory aggregation, persists into pluggable storage, and returns through the GraphQL query layer. One caveat, verified against the repository: since SkyWalking 9 the Java agent lives in the sibling repo apache/skywalking-java; the repo explored here holds the OAP server, protocols, and the analysis engine.

Why does this matter for AI workloads? Because the core has grown first-class concepts for them. server-core contains AIAgentSessionFlowRecord, annotated for the AI_AGENT_SESSION_FLOW scope, and GenAIEvaluationRecord, which stores GenAI evaluation results as queryable data. In other words, the same engine that aggregates service latency also aggregates token usage and evaluation outcomes, so an LLM gateway can be debugged with the same tools as the REST services behind it. Observability platforms are quietly becoming control planes for LLM applications, and these record types are where that convergence shows up in code.

The ten-thousand-meter view: receivers ingest agent and OTLP traffic on the left, the analysis core turns telemetry into Metrics, L1/L2 workers aggregate and persist, and the query module serves GraphQL on the right.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Every gRPC endpoint is published through a shared server: receivers register on the GRPCHandlerRegister, L26 interface.
  • The trace entry point is TraceSegmentReportServiceHandler, L39; its streaming collect (L63) forwards each segment to the parser via send (L73).
  • OpenTelemetryMetricHandler, L38 accepts OTLP export (L74) — so any OpenTelemetry SDK, including ones on Python or Go AI services, can feed SkyWalking.
  • DispatcherManager.forward, L45 routes parsed sources to OAL-generated dispatchers by scope.
  • All metric types extend abstract Metrics, L41, whose combine (L68) is the merge primitive everything builds on.
  • MetricsStreamProcessor.in, L141 is the hot path handing each metric to its per-class L1 worker; create (L165) assembles that chain at registration.
  • The query side composes one executable schema in GraphQLQueryProvider.prepare, L102.

The detailed view: shared gRPC/HTTP registries, trace and OTLP receivers, the OAL dispatch layer, L1 aggregation workers, L2 persistence workers, and the GraphQL stack, with paths verified on master.

A Module System All the Way Down

The backend is a module container, not one big application class. Each capability is a ModuleDefine plus a ModuleProvider resolved at boot; the central CoreModule, L82 declares the name "core" on L83, with storage, query, telemetry, and analyzer modules plugging alongside. A starter module assembles the chosen providers into a runnable server, which is why the same codebase powers both a full application server and lighter deployment modes. That indirection is why storage backends are swappable — providers are looked up by interface, never hard-wired.

Receiver wiring shows the payoff. TraceModuleProvider.start() on L62 fetches the shared GRPCHandlerRegister and adds its handlers; the OTLP provider (L38) does the same. One process exposes many ingestion protocols on shared ports with no per-receiver socket code.

Receivers: Where Telemetry Enters

Receivers are deliberately thin. The streaming trace handler wraps its parse call in a histogram timer and error counter, so ingestion latency is itself a SkyWalking metric — the codebase observes itself, which matters when you are diagnosing the diagnostician during a traffic storm. A REST twin exists for gRPC-blocked environments (TraceSegmentReportHandler, L38), and a compatibility handler keeps older agent protocol versions alive.

The OTLP receiver matters most for AI infrastructure. It delegates to OpenTelemetryMetricRequestProcessor.processMetricsRequest, L149, replaying samples through registered MAL converters — Meter Analysis Language rules that translate arbitrary OTLP gauges into SkyWalking metrics. If you already push metrics from an inference gateway, the same traffic lands here via a rule file instead of new code. The repo also ships Zipkin ingestion modules, which pairs nicely with our Zipkin architecture tour when consolidating an existing trace estate.

OAL and the Two-Level Metrics Aggregation

This is the heart. OAL, the Open Assessment Language, is SkyWalking’s answer to the question every APM eventually faces: how do you turn an unbounded firehose of raw spans into a bounded set of aggregate metrics without hand-writing aggregation code per feature? The answer is a small declarative language whose script files name the metrics, their scopes, and their functions, and a compiler that turns those declarations into ordinary Java classes at build time. At runtime, DispatcherManager.forward, L45 calls the dispatchers registered for a source’s scope — the generated SegmentDispatcher.dispatch, L29 handles raw traces, which end as SegmentRecords, L47, persisted through the record stream.

Metrics take a two-level ride, and the class comments in the source describe the design candidly. L1 is in-memory merging: MetricsAggregateWorker (L57) shares one adaptive queue across metric types, accepts items at in, L146, merges them in a MergableBufferedData.accept, L49 cache keyed by entity and time bucket, and pushes merged buckets onward in flush (L178). In a cluster, MetricsRemoteWorker, L33 ships each bucket to the node owning its hash slot, so aggregation work is distributed across the OAP nodes instead of hammering one of them.

L2 is persistence. MetricsPersistentWorker.in (L172) buffers metrics in a 70-second session cache so repeated writes to one entity collapse into a single database operation, and buildBatchRequests (L188) turns expired sessions into batch writes through IBatchDAO, L30, the interface every storage plugin implements. Down-sampling is explicit: Metrics demands toHour (L80) and toDay (L87) clones, and a transitive worker fans minute data to hour and day workers. Streams register storage models through the ModelRegistry, L33 interface. The same write-amplification-versus-read-speed tension we studied in Grafana Mimir and Tempo reappears here — solved inside the application instead of the database.

From Install to Your First Model

Getting a live topology takes two downloads. First, start the OAP server and UI from the distribution built from this repo’s apm-dist module; the documented defaults are gRPC ingestion on 11800, HTTP on 12800, UI on 8080. Second, attach the agent from apache/skywalking-java to your JVM-based AI service:

java -javaagent:/opt/skywalking-agent/skywalking-agent.jar \
     -Dskywalking.agent.service_name=inference-gateway \
     -Dskywalking.collector.backend_service=oap:11800 \
     -jar inference-gateway.jar

Refresh the UI and the topology appears — nodes for your services, edges for their calls, latency percentiles per endpoint, all derived from the segments your first requests produced. No code changes, no SDK calls. If you prefer containers, the repo’s docker directory and the published images let you run the OAP server and UI as two containers with a shared network, which is convenient when the observability stack should live and die with a Kubernetes namespace rather than a host. For the non-JVM parts of the AI stack — a Python model server, a Go preprocessor — point an OpenTelemetry SDK at the OTLP receiver above; the OpenTelemetry Collector can sit in front as a buffer for retries and multiplexing. Minutes later you have what every ML platform team needs: which endpoint is slow, whether errors cluster on a dependency, and how AI-agent sessions actually flow through the system.

Querying: GraphQL and MQE

Everything the UI renders arrives through one protocol. The QueryModule, L26 defines the "query" module; the GraphQL provider’s prepare() composes the schema file by file — metadata, topology, traces, logs, alarms, profiling, AI-agent conversations — and start() (L176) mounts the executable schema as GraphQLQueryHandler, L41 behind the shared HTTP registry.

Beneath the resolvers sit plain services: TraceQueryService.queryBasicTraces (L119) pages through stored summaries, TopologyQueryService.getGlobalTopology (L92) assembles the service graph, and MetricsQueryService, L44 serves metric series. The twist since 9.5 is MQE, a Metrics Query Expression language evaluated by MQEExecutor, L52 at query time — dashboards can compute ratios like p99-latency-per-request without new storage code. Because the schema is introspectable GraphQL, you can also query it from any client: a notebook, a CI job that fails when error rates cross a threshold, or a custom SRE bot that pulls topology snapshots into your chat tool.

Honest Limits

Everything above is limited to what the source and repository layout support; no benchmarks were run for this article. First, this repo does not contain the Java agent — since the 9.x split, Byte Buddy instrumentation and agent configuration live in apache/skywalking-java, so agent behavior belongs to that project’s source, and any statement about which frameworks it instruments should be checked against its documentation. Second, the numbers quoted (a 20,000-slot L1 buffer, a 500 ms flush period, a 70-second session) are source-level defaults in the cited classes; they are tunable, and real behavior under your traffic is knowable only from your load tests. Third, aggregation relies on OAL code generated at build time — generated dispatcher classes do not exist in the source tree until you build the project, and reading master means reading a moving target, so treat line numbers here as a snapshot of one commit rather than a stable API. Fourth, the AI-agent and GenAI record types are present and queryable, but how well they model real LLM workloads is a question only your data can answer. Finally, the IBatchDAO contract is backend-agnostic by design, so any performance statement about BanyanDB or Elasticsearch must come from those implementations’ own documentation, never from this tour.
entry.summary: A guided source-code tour of Apache SkyWalking's OAP server, from gRPC receivers through two-level metrics aggregation to the GraphQL query layer.

entry.title: Telegraf Under the Hood: The Plugin-Driven Go Agent That Moves Your Metrics

link.title: Telegraf Under the Hood: The Plugin-Driven Go Agent That Moves Your Metrics

entry.content:
Training and serving AI models is a telemetry problem as much as a compute problem. A training run is only as trustworthy as the numbers you can see while it happens: GPU utilization and memory pressure from every node, host CPU and disk saturation, container restarts, queue lag on the data-loading side, and the request-rate/latency pairs that tell you whether an LLM endpoint is healthy. Telegraf, InfluxData’s agent for collecting, processing, aggregating, and writing metrics, is one of the standard answers to that problem — the README describes a suite of over 300 plugins built by more than 1,200 contributors, shipped as a single static Go binary configured with TOML.

For AI and ML infrastructure specifically, the plugin catalog maps almost one-to-one onto the telemetry you need. The inputs.nvidia_smi plugin scrapes GPU health straight from nvidia-smi on training boxes. inputs.docker watches the containers your serving stack lives in. inputs.prometheus pulls metrics from anything that exposes a scrape endpoint, which is how most modern inference servers report. inputs.http_listener_v2 and the OpenTelemetry input accept pushed data from instrumented services, while inputs.kafka_consumer and inputs.mqtt_consumer tap event streams at the edge. On the far side, output plugins ship the result to InfluxDB, expose it for Prometheus, forward it over HTTP, or write it anywhere else you have wired a backend such as InfluxDB or Prometheus.

What makes Telegraf worth reading at the source level is how small the core is compared to what it does. The whole system rests on four plugin interfaces, one channel-carrying agent loop, and a buffering layer that turns flaky writes into at-least-once delivery. This post walks the current master tree with line-anchored links to every claim, using diagrams generated directly from the repository structure.

Overview of the Telegraf flow: polled and service inputs feed an accumulator, metrics travel through processors and aggregators, then land in per-output buffers that flush to backends. Generated from the influxdata/telegraf source tree.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Entry and wiring. Agent.Run, L110 initializes every plugin, then starts outputs first, walks back through aggregators and processors, and finally launches the inputs — building the channel graph from the sink side so nothing emits into a closed channel.
  • Two input styles. Polled plugins like inputs.cpu implement Input with Gather, L3; long-running receivers implement ServiceInput, L11, which adds Start/Stop so an HTTP server can run inside the agent process.
  • One accumulator per plugin. Each plugin receives an Accumulator, L8; the agent’s implementation (NewAccumulator, L22) applies timestamp rounding and pushes typed Metric values into the channel.
  • A goroutine and a ticker per input. runInputs, L380 gives every input its own interval, jitter, and offset; gatherLoop, L548 ticks forever while gatherOnce, L569 warns when a collection overruns its slot.
  • Inline transforms. Processors implement Processor.Apply, L6 for synchronous mutation, and the agent pumps metrics through the chain in runProcessors, L632.
  • Windowed aggregation. Aggregators implement Aggregator, L7 with Add/Push/Reset; the agent drives their period windows in runAggregators, L668.
  • Buffered delivery. Outputs are wrapped by a RunningOutput that keeps a Buffer, L60 of unsent metrics and requeues whatever a backend rejects.
  • Periodic flush. flushLoop, L872 wakes each output on its flush interval, on a flush signal, or when a batch-size threshold fires.

Internals of Telegraf: the CLI hands a loaded config to the agent, which wires running plugins, metric contracts, and example plugins into one running system. Generated from the influxdata/telegraf source tree.

The Four Plugin Contracts

Everything in plugins/ exists to satisfy one of four small Go interfaces, plus a handful of optional capability interfaces. Inputs expose Gather(Accumulator) error and are called once per interval. Outputs expose Connect, Write(metrics []Metric), and Close in Output, L3, and the agent guarantees Write is never called concurrently, so plugins need no locking. Processors are synchronous by default, but stateful, asynchronous transforms can implement StreamingProcessor, L14, which gets a Start/Add/Stop lifecycle instead of a pure function.

The metric itself is the second half of the contract. Metric, L37 carries a name, ordered tags and fields, a timestamp, and a ValueType — the enum covers Counter, Gauge, Untyped, Summary, and Histogram. Delivery is explicit: Accept, Reject, and Drop mark what happened to a metric after the last stage touched it. Plugins that ingest arbitrary payloads can also attach a Parser, L6 (Parse/ParseLine) on the way in, and outputs convert metrics to wire formats through a Serializer, L8 with a batch variant. That separation is why the same CPU plugin can write to any of the dozens of registered outputs without either side knowing the other exists.

Inside the Agent Loop

The runtime heart is agent/agent.go. After InitPlugins, L208 calls Init on everything, startOutputs, L769 connects each output once — a failed connect is retried after fifteen seconds before the agent gives up on that plugin. The channel stages are wired sink-first: startProcessors, L598 iterates the processor list backwards so that config order becomes data order, and startInputs, L330 starts only the service inputs, handing each a dedicated accumulator whose precision rules differ from the polled ones.

The gather side is deliberately defensive. Each input gets its own goroutine and ticker; gatherOnce runs the plugin’s Gather in a child goroutine and logs a warning every interval that the collection fails to finish, while the loop skips the next scheduled tick if the previous one is still running. A deferred panicRecover turns a panicking plugin into a logged fatal error instead of a dead agent. On the output side, runOutputs, L817 fans every metric out to all outputs — copying for all but the last one — and the per-output flush timer is complemented by BatchReady, which lets batch-oriented outputs flush early. There are also single-shot modes: Test prints one gather’s worth of line-protocol to stdout, and Once runs a full cycle and fails if any output still holds unsent metrics.

Windows, Batches, and Delivery Tracking

Aggregation and buffering are where Telegraf earns its reliability. An aggregator’s window is initialized before the first Add and re-armed after every Push, L180; the push loop sleeps until each window ends rather than using a drifting ticker. Metrics matched by an aggregator are dropped from the main flow, everything else passes through untouched — aggregation augments the stream, it does not gate it.

Output delivery is transactional. RunningOutput.Write, L302 starts a transaction from the buffer, serializes the batch through the output’s serializer, and calls the plugin’s Write; whatever the backend accepts is removed, and the rest stays queued for the next attempt. The Buffer interface, L60 abstracts that queue, and its factory selects one of three strategies: in-memory by default, a disk write-through variant, or a discard mode that sheds load. Batch size and buffer capacity come straight from the agent settings MetricBatchSize and MetricBufferLimit. For stronger guarantees, a plugin can ask for a TrackingAccumulator, L81, which returns a delivery signal once a tracked metric or group has been fully processed — the mechanism transactional inputs use to know when it is safe to acknowledge upstream.

Config as the Composition Root

A Telegraf process is the evaluated result of its TOML files. NewConfig builds the defaults, AgentConfig, L184 holds the global knobs — interval, round-interval, flush interval, batch size, buffer limit — and LoadAll, L571 loads one or many files, from local paths or URLs. Each [[inputs.*]] / [[outputs.*]] table becomes a running plugin through addInput/addOutput and their processor and aggregator siblings, which also wire name filters, aliases, and per-plugin overrides. The CLI layer in cmd/telegraf then ties it together: runAgent constructs the agent, and reloadLoop tears it down and rebuilds it whenever a SIGHUP arrives or a watched config file changes, which is how you add a GPU node’s input set without reimaging the box.

From Install to Your First Model

The quickest verified path from zero to a running collector uses Docker. Pull the image, write a minimal TOML file, and run it with your config mounted:

docker pull telegraf

[[inputs.cpu]]
[[inputs.mem]]
[[outputs.file]]

docker run --rm --volume $PWD/config.toml:/etc/telegraf/telegraf.conf telegraf

That exact configuration is the quick start in the repository docs: two polled inputs and the file output, which prints line protocol to stdout so you can see your first metrics within seconds. From there, the upgrade path for an ML host is mechanical. Replace outputs.file with outputs.influxdb_v2 or outputs.prometheus_client to feed a real backend, and add [[inputs.nvidia_smi]] on any GPU box to start collecting utilization, memory, temperature, and power metrics per device. For binaries and packages beyond Docker, the repository’s install guide covers package managers, tarballs, and Windows builds. If you are standing up the receiving side too, InfluxDB is the natural first target, and a Prometheus endpoint is the pragmatic choice when your dashboards already live there — both are sink outputs, so the agent config changes by one table.

Honest Limits

Measured against what ML teams often expect, Telegraf has real boundaries. It is a collection and routing agent, not storage: without a backend output it holds data only in buffers, and the buffer contract means oldest unsent metrics are evicted under sustained pressure once the configured limit is hit. Aggregation is period-windowed by design; if you need event-by-event enrichment or routing decisions, that is processor work, not aggregator work. A hung Gather does not crash the agent, but it does starve that one input’s slot — the loop warns and skips, it does not preempt the plugin. The agent is also a compiled binary, so adopting a plugin not in the release means building your own binary from the tree. Finally, the project’s own docs are candid that plugin depth varies across the 300-plus catalog, and each plugin’s README is the source of truth for its settings and quirks. None of these are disqualifying — they are the trade-offs of a single-binary, config-first collector — but knowing them up front is the difference between a telemetry stack you trust and one you debug at 2 a.m.
entry.summary: A line-anchored source tour of influxdata/telegraf: the four plugin contracts, the agent loop, windowed aggregation, buffered writes, and what a 300-plugin collection agent can and cannot do.

entry.title: Grafana Tempo Under the Hood: Kafka, Block Builders and a TraceQL Engine That Speaks Parquet

link.title: Grafana Tempo Under the Hood: Kafka, Block Builders and a TraceQL Engine That Speaks Parquet

entry.content:
An AI application in 2026 is not one program. It is a chain: a router picks a model, a retriever fetches context from a vector store, an inference server runs the prompt, tool calls fan out to external APIs, and a post-processor stitches everything into an answer. When that chain gets slow or silently drops a step, logs and metrics tell you that something broke — only distributed tracing tells you where. Traces attach a single ID to every hop, so a 12-second agent turn decomposes into retriever latency, queue time, token generation and the one misconfigured retry loop that caused it all.

Grafana Tempo is the tracing backend built for that job at scale. Its README is blunt about the design bet: an “open source, easy-to-use, and high-scale distributed tracing backend” that is “cost-efficient, requiring only object storage to operate.” No indexing service, no search cluster — traces land in S3, GCS, Azure Blob or local disk, and queries either hit a trace ID directly or use TraceQL, a traces-first query language inspired by LogQL and PromQL. Tempo accepts Jaeger, Zipkin, Kafka and OpenTelemetry formats, which makes it a natural landing zone next to your OpenTelemetry collector.

This post is a source tour of Tempo’s main branch as of today (commit tree read on 2026-11-05). The codebase has drifted in a fascinating way: the classic “distributor / ingester / querier” trio from Tempo’s early years is gone. There is no ingester directory left in the tree at all. The write path is now distributor → Kafka → block-builder → object storage, with a live store serving the hot window, and background backend scheduler/worker modules doing compaction chores. Everything below cites verified symbols and line numbers from the Go source, and the two diagrams were generated from the same tree.

Overview of Tempo on main: one binary that composes a distributor, a Kafka-fed write path, a live store for recent traces, a tempodb layer over pluggable object storage, and a query path where TraceQL is evaluated against both live and block data.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Everything starts in main, L47: it parses config, registers a gogocodec for protobuf efficiency, and hands targets like all, distributor, block-builder, live-store or query-frontend to a dskit module manager (the target constants live in modules.go, L71).
  • The Distributor, L219 terminates inbound traces through PushTraces, PushTraces, L475, after an embedded OpenTelemetry receiver shim (receiversShim, receiversShim, L124) has already normalized OTLP traffic.
  • requestsByTraceID, L741 rebatches incoming spans by trace ID — the unit of storage and retrieval for everything downstream.
  • The distributor then publishes PushBytesRequest records to Kafka via sendToKafka, L665 (the message shape is declared in tempo.proto, L349).
  • On the consuming side, the BlockBuilder, L99 runs as Kafka consumer group block-builder and cuts a block roughly every 10 seconds (cutTime is a constant in that file).
  • Writes stage through a WAL: WAL, L24 buffers traces on local disk, and RescanBlocks (RescanBlocks, L79) recovers in-flight blocks after a crash or restart.
  • The LiveStore, L127 keeps the most recent window queryable the moment spans arrive — it serves PushBytes, FindTraceByID and SearchRecent directly.
  • Storage is centralized in New, L181, which returns the Reader/Writer/Compactor trio over backend interfaces (Reader, L68 and Writer, L46) implemented for S3, GCS, Azure and local disk.
  • Queries flow through the QueryFrontend, L49 into the Querier, L72, which compiles TraceQL in the Engine, L26 with Compile (Compile, L33).

The detailed view: module wiring, the distributor's internal push targets, the Kafka decode path, block building through the WAL, live-store components, tempodb plus backends, vParquet5 compaction, and the full query path including backend scheduler and worker.

The Distributor: One Door, Many Formats

The distributor is deliberately thin. Inbound OTLP is handled by a shim that hosts real OpenTelemetry Collector receivers inside the Tempo process: New (New, L158) builds the shim, and ConsumeTraces (ConsumeTraces, L346) is the sink every receiver pushes into. Conversion to Tempo’s internal protobuf is direct — directTraces (directTraces, L15) walks the pdata trees and builds tempopb structures without an intermediate serialization round trip.

Two details reveal how the team thinks about scale. First, the distributor ring uses a single token (ringNumTokens = 1); a comment in the source explains the ring exists “for HealthyInstancesCount (global ingestion-rate divisor), not sharding” — sharding is Kafka’s job now. Second, per-tenant enforcement happens before anything is accepted: checkForRateLimits (checkForRateLimits, L434) applies rate and size limits, and the module also fans spans out to the metrics generator via sendToGenerators (sendToGenerators, L633) and into the live store via pushTracesToLiveStore (pushTracesToLiveStore, L606).

Kafka Is the Spine of the Write Path

The old ingester’s job — receive spans, buffer them, periodically flush immutable blocks — is split across three modules. The distributor serializes each rebatched batch into a PushBytesRequest and publishes it keyed by trace ID. A small pkg/ingest package owns the wire protocol: Decoder.Decode (Decode, L137) turns Kafka records back into protobuf, while PartitionOffsetClient (PartitionOffsetClient, L24) tracks committed offsets so ownership can move between block-builders without data loss or duplicates.

The block-builder then does what an ingester used to do, but stateless-with-replay: its consumer group id is literally block-builder, and cutTime is 10 seconds. Inside, a partition writer routes records per tenant (writer.pushBytes, pushBytes, L64), a per-tenant tenantStore appends traces into the WAL (AppendTrace, AppendTrace, L92), and on each cycle Flush (Flush, L115) cuts an immutable block and hands it to a WriteableBlock whose Write (Write, L46) persists it through tempodb. Kafka’s log plus the WAL give you two layers of durability; the partition-reader in the live store (PartitionReader, PartitionReader, L33) replays the same records so recent traces are searchable instantly.

Object storage stays dumb by design. Every tenant’s block list is materialized in a TenantIndex (newTenantIndex, L22) written to the backend, so readers never list buckets. Heavyweight chores — compaction, retention — are queued by the BackendScheduler (BackendScheduler, L39) and executed by the BackendWorker (BackendWorker, L43), keeping the hot write path free of background I/O storms. This is the same “objects plus index” philosophy you’ll find in MinIO-centered stacks (see our /minio/ tour) and in event-log systems like /kafka/.

TraceQL: Predicates That Fall Down Into Parquet

Tempo’s query story is TraceQL. Parsing starts at Parse (Parse, L26), which lexes and parses a query into a RootExpr; Compile then optimizes it into executable stages. The engine evaluates queries over Spanset values (Spanset, L231) — sets of spans that flow through filter stages until the final response.

The clever part is where evaluation happens. Blocks are stored in the vParquet5 format, whose schema lays out Span fields as typed columns (Span, L204). Each block exposes a span facade with AttributeFor (AttributeFor, L148) so TraceQL predicates can be pushed down into column pruning and page indexes rather than materializing every span. The querier stitches this together: FindTraceByID (FindTraceByID, L200) consults the live-store ring first, then the block store; SearchRecent (SearchRecent, L372) and SearchBlock (SearchBlock, L654) shard search across many blocks in parallel behind the query frontend.

From Install to Your First Model

Tempo ships as a single Go binary and a grafana/tempo Docker image; the README points to the getting-started docs and to deployment examples in the repository. The fastest reproducible route: clone the repo, enter example/docker-compose/distributed/, and run Docker Compose — the verified files there include tempo.yaml, a Grafana datasource file, an Alloy collector config (config.alloy), and even a redpanda-console.yaml, which tells you how central the event log is to the current design. For a no-Kafka start, the all target runs every module in one process, and the distributor has a local push path (pushLocal, pushLocal, L588) that skips the broker entirely.

Now trace something you care about — an LLM chain is perfect because every hop is a span. Point any OTLP-instrumented app (a Python agent framework, a FastAPI service behind an API gateway, or your existing setup from our /opentelemetry-collector/ walkthrough) at the collector endpoint the compose file exposes. If you already push spans from /jaeger/ SDKs or a Jaeger agent, Tempo speaks those formats too. Give the root span an attribute like demo=true so it is easy to find.

Then query it. TraceQL is reachable from Grafana’s Explore UI or straight over HTTP at /api/search (the constant PathSearch in http.go, L86); a first query as simple as { span.demo = true } returns matching traces with timing and attributes per hop. To check the binary itself, /api/echo is the health ping. From there, refine: filter by duration, count spans per service, or switch to trace-by-ID lookups once your AI platform logs the trace_id next to each model call — that ID is the join key between your application logs and Tempo.

Honest Limits

What follows is only what the source or README supports — no invented benchmarks. First, this architecture is visibly in motion: the block-builder carries a TODO questioning whether its WAL handle should be per tenant, and the querier still contains a helper named postProcessIngesterSearchResults (postProcessIngesterSearchResults, L900) — legacy naming from the pre-Kafka era. Expect churn on main.

Second, read the README’s “requiring only object storage” claim in context: the code paths we traced show that the distributed write path sends every record through Kafka, and the shipped distributed compose file runs Redpanda alongside Tempo. The single-binary all target with local push avoids that dependency, but a scaled deployment should budget for operating an event log, not just a bucket. Third, TraceQL metrics are labeled experimental in the README, so treat aggregate-latency dashboards built on them as directional rather than SLA-grade. Finally, my diagrams and line references describe main on 2026-11-05; Tempo moves fast, so treat the links as a snapshot, and verify against your checked-out version before quoting internals in design reviews.
entry.summary: A source-code tour of Grafana Tempo's Go internals: the distributor, the Kafka write path, block builders, the live store, vParquet compaction and the TraceQL engine.

entry.title: Vector: The Rust Router That Moves Your LLM’s Logs, Metrics, and Traces

link.title: Vector: The Rust Router That Moves Your LLM’s Logs, Metrics, and Traces

entry.content:
Ask anyone running a large language model service what their telemetry situation looks like and watch them wince. A single serving cluster can emit millions of structured log lines per day — prompts, completions, tool calls, guardrail verdicts — plus metrics like tokens per second, time to first token, and GPU utilization, plus traces for every step an agent takes. Where all of that lands, and at what fidelity, decides whether you can debug a regression at 3 a.m. or only guess at it. Vector, maintained by Datadog under the vectordotdev organization, is the Rust-powered engine that has become one of the most credible answers to that routing problem.

The README’s opening describes Vector as a high-performance, end-to-end agent and aggregator for observability data that lets you collect, transform, and route your logs and metrics to any vendor you want today — and any other vendor tomorrow. Three claims matter for AI infrastructure work. First, reliability: the project states that its primary design goal is reliability, and it is built in memory-safe Rust. Second, reach: the README reports over 100,000 downloads per day and a largest user processing more than 500 terabytes daily.
